clinicalPearls: Vasculitis is inflammation of and damage to blood vessel walls that typically narrows the lumen and produces downstream tissue ischemia; it may be the sole disease, may be secondary to another disease, and may be single-organ or multisystem.

Suspect vasculitis in any unexplained systemic illness; clinical clues include palpable purpura, pulmonary infiltrates with microscopic hematuria, chronic sinusitis, mononeuritis multiplex, unexplained ischemic events, and glomerulonephritis with multisystem disease.

Definitive diagnosis usually rests on biopsy of clinically involved tissue; 'blind' biopsy of organs without subjective or objective involvement has very low yield and should be avoided. Catheter-directed arteriography is used when PAN, Takayasu, or primary CNS vasculitis is suspected.

ANCA subtypes: cANCA targets proteinase-3 (>90% positive in active granulomatosis with polyangiitis); pANCA most relevantly targets myeloperoxidase (variably positive in microscopic polyangiitis, EGPA, and isolated necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis). Only anti-MPO and anti-PR3 are convincingly vasculitis-associated.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis classically combines granulomatous vasculitis of the upper and lower respiratory tracts with glomerulonephritis; upper airway involvement occurs in ~95% and renal disease (~77% over course) dominates prognosis. Renal lesion is pauci-immune (no immune-complex deposition).

Microscopic polyangiitis resembles GPA but lacks granulomatous inflammation; it favors small vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles), with glomerulonephritis in at least 79% and alveolar hemorrhage in ~12%. Upper airway disease and lung nodules are atypical and, if present, point instead to GPA. ANCA (usually anti-MPO) in ~75%.

EGPA (Churg-Strauss) is defined by asthma, blood and tissue eosinophilia, and vasculitis; eosinophilia exceeds 1000 cells/uL in >80% and ANCA (usually anti-MPO) is present in ~48%. Cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death, so echocardiography is advised at diagnosis.

Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotizing vasculitis of small- and medium-sized muscular arteries that spares pulmonary arteries and does NOT cause glomerulonephritis, granuloma, or significant eosinophilia; renal involvement is arteritis (microaneurysms, hypertension), not glomerular. ANCA are rarely found; screen all patients for hepatitis B and C.

Giant cell arteritis occurs almost exclusively after age 50, presents with fever, anemia, high ESR/CRP, and headache; ischemic optic neuropathy with sudden blindness is the dreaded complication, and patients carry an ~18-fold increased risk of thoracic aortic aneurysm. Treatment should not be delayed for biopsy.

Polymyalgia rheumatica (aching/stiffness of neck, shoulder and hip girdles with raised ESR/CRP) coexists with GCA in 40-50% of GCA patients; creatine kinase is normal and RF/anti-CCP should be negative. ~10-20% with isolated PMR later develop GCA.

Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel panarteritis with strong predilection for the aortic arch and its branches, classically in adolescent girls and young women; suspect it in a young woman with diminished or absent pulses, an interarm blood-pressure discrepancy, or arterial bruits.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein) is a small-vessel, immune-complex (IgA) vasculitis most common in children 4-7 years, with palpable purpura over buttocks/lower limbs, arthralgias, colicky GI symptoms (intussusception risk), and usually mild self-limited glomerulonephritis; serum complement is normal and IgA is elevated in about half.

Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis is most often associated with hepatitis C (estimated in ~5% of chronic HCV); rheumatoid factor is almost always present, hypocomplementemia occurs in ~90%, and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis accounts for ~80% of renal lesions.

Temporal artery biopsy yield improves with a 3-5 cm segment and serial sectioning because involvement is segmental; biopsy may still show arteritis after about 14 days of glucocorticoid therapy, so starting treatment promptly does not preclude later diagnosis.
harrison.pathophysiology: Most vasculitic syndromes are thought to be at least partly immune-mediated responses to antigenic stimuli, with the precise mechanism varying by disease. Three principal hypothesized mechanisms are recognized. (1) Pathogenic immune-complex formation/deposition (e.g., IgA vasculitis, lupus vasculitis, serum-sickness/cutaneous syndromes, HCV-associated cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, HBV-associated vasculitis): antigen-antibody complexes formed in antigen excess deposit in vessel walls whose permeability has been raised by vasoactive amines, activate complement (notably chemotactic C5a), recruit neutrophils that phagocytose complexes and release intracytoplasmic enzymes damaging the wall, with later mononuclear infiltration and luminal compromise. (2) ANCA production (GPA, microscopic polyangiitis, EGPA): when neutrophils/monocytes are primed by TNF-alpha or IL-1 or alternative-complement activation, PR3 and MPO translocate to the cell membrane where ANCA can engage them, triggering degranulation, reactive oxygen species, endothelial injury, and release of IL-1/IL-8; however, some patients have active GPA without ANCA and titers correlate poorly with activity, so a primary pathogenic role remains debated. (3) Pathogenic T-lymphocyte responses and granuloma formation (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, GPA, EGPA): cytokine-activated endothelium expresses HLA class II and secretes IL-1, enabling CD4+ T-cell interactions; IL-1 and TNF-alpha upregulate ELAM-1 and VCAM-1 to enhance leukocyte adhesion. In GCA the disease is antigen-driven, with clonally restricted T cells suggesting an arterial-wall antigen, and both TH1 (IFN-gamma) and TH17 (IL-17) CD4 lineages contribute. The size, type, and location of affected vessels, host genetic predisposition, environmental exposures, reticuloendothelial clearance of complexes, hemodynamic factors, and endothelial integrity all influence the ultimate phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Other primary vasculitides when the full classic syndrome is incomplete
Connective tissue disease-associated (lupus, rheumatoid, sarcoid) vasculitis
Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis or other inflammatory arthropathy (vs polymyalgia rheumatica)
Lymphomatoid granulomatosis and extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (vs GPA midline destructive disease)
infectionMimics: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and rhinoscleroma (midline destructive mimics of GPA)
nonInfectiousMimics: Drug toxicity (cocaine, levamisole-adulterated cocaine, amphetamines, ergot alkaloids, methysergide, arsenic)
additionalInvestigations: Tissue biopsy of clinically involved organ (highest yield: lung for GPA; symptomatic skin nodules, painful testes, or nerve/muscle for PAN)
ANCA testing (anti-PR3 / cANCA and anti-MPO / pANCA) with awareness of variable predictive value by presentation
Catheter-directed (dye) arteriography for suspected PAN; MR or CT arteriography of aorta and branches for Takayasu and large-vessel GCA
Temporal artery biopsy (3-5 cm with serial sections) and/or temporal +/- axillary artery ultrasound 'halo' sign for GCA
ESR and/or CRP, complete blood count (anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, eosinophilia in EGPA)
Urinalysis for hematuria, proteinuria, and red-cell casts; serum creatinine
Hepatitis B and C serologies/RNA (PAN, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis)
Serum cryoglobulins, rheumatoid factor, and complement levels for cryoglobulinemic vasculitis
Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence (IgA and C3 deposition in IgA vasculitis; leukocytoclastic vasculitis in cutaneous vasculitis)
Echocardiography at diagnosis in EGPA given cardiac mortality risk
Consider DADA2 (adenosine deaminase type 2 deficiency) evaluation in early-onset PAN-like vasculitis
redFlags: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis or rising creatinine (GPA, microscopic polyangiitis, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis)
Hemoptysis / diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (microscopic polyangiitis, GPA)
New or worsening headache, jaw or tongue claudication, scalp tenderness, or any visual symptom in a patient over 50 (impending GCA-related blindness)
Subglottic stenosis or progressive airway obstruction in GPA
Abdominal pain with GI bleeding suggesting bowel infarction/perforation (PAN, EGPA, IgA vasculitis with intussusception)
Cardiac involvement (myocarditis/coronary vasculitis) in EGPA or PAN
Interarm blood-pressure discrepancy, absent pulses, or aortic aneurysm/dissection in large-vessel disease
Concurrent anti-GBM antibody positivity in ANCA-associated vasculitis
harrison.prognosis: Outcome varies markedly by syndrome and by treatment. Untreated granulomatosis with polyangiitis was once uniformly fatal within months; modern cyclophosphamide- or rituximab-based regimens with glucocorticoids achieve improvement in >90% and remission in ~75%, with 5-year survival >80%, though 50-70% of remissions are followed by relapse and many patients accrue irreversible damage (renal insufficiency, hearing loss, subglottic stenosis, saddle-nose deformity). Treated microscopic polyangiitis has ~74% 5-year survival with relapse in at least 34%, mortality from alveolar hemorrhage or GI/cardiac/renal disease. Untreated EGPA has a ~25% 5-year survival; with treatment about 72% survive at 78 months, and myocardial involvement causes ~39% of deaths. Untreated PAN carries a 10-20% 5-year survival (death from bowel infarction/perforation and cardiovascular causes); combination immunosuppression markedly improves survival, with relapse in ~10-20%. GCA seldom causes acute death but carries late risk of aortic aneurysm rupture/dissection; PMR generally responds well. Takayasu is usually chronic and relapsing with widely variable reported survival. IgA vasculitis prognosis is excellent (mortality exceedingly rare; 1-5% of children reach end-stage renal disease, possibly higher in adults; recurrences in 10-40%). In cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, glomerulonephritis is a poor prognostic sign (~15% progress to end-stage renal disease, 40% of whom later die of cardiovascular disease, infection, or liver failure).
pitfalls: Do NOT treat a rise in ANCA titer alone as evidence of relapse; only ~43% of patients relapsed within a year of an ANCA rise, and many remain ANCA-positive for years in remission.

ANCA predictive value falls sharply when renal disease is absent (~30-60% with sinus/lung-only disease vs ~90% with active glomerulonephritis), so biopsy is needed to exclude infection or malignancy that can cause false-positive ANCA.

Upper airway lesions in GPA should NEVER be irradiated; midline destructive disease mimics include NK/T-cell lymphoma and cocaine/levamisole injury (anti-neutrophil-elastase ANCA, granulocytopenia point to levamisole).
Eosinophilia is rare in PAN; when markedly elevated it should redirect toward EGPA.
In PAN, MR and CT arteriography lack the resolution to visualize the small/medium aneurysms, so catheter-directed dye arteriography is required.
When tocilizumab or other IL-6 blockade is used in GCA, ESR and CRP normalize and can no longer be used to gauge disease activity or detect infection.
TMP-SMX should never be used alone to treat active GPA involving organs beyond the sinonasal tissue.
Failure to exclude infection (especially endocarditis) before starting empirical immunosuppression in a rapidly deteriorating patient can be catastrophic.
Glucocorticoids do not reliably benefit the skin or renal disease of IgA vasculitis and do not shorten its course or reduce recurrence.
harrison.severityClassification: For ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA/microscopic polyangiitis), Harrison frames management by severe vs nonsevere disease. Severe disease involves life- or organ-threatening manifestations and is judged by both extent and the specific organ affected: pulmonary disease may be nonsevere (nodules without respiratory compromise) or severe (alveolar hemorrhage), whereas active glomerulonephritis is ALWAYS considered severe even when renal function is normal. Treatment is conceptually divided into a remission-induction phase followed by a maintenance phase, with regimen choice stratified by this severity assessment along with relapse history and comorbidities.
management: Induce remission in severe, organ-threatening ANCA-associated vasculitis with high-dose glucocorticoids combined with either rituximab or cyclophosphamide
Maintain remission with rituximab, azathioprine or methotrexate while tapering glucocorticoids to the lowest effective dose
Add plasma exchange in selected cases such as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis or alveolar haemorrhage
Treat the underlying trigger: antiviral therapy for hepatitis-B- or hepatitis-C-associated (cryoglobulinaemic) vasculitis, and withdrawal of the offending agent in drug-induced disease
Start glucocorticoids urgently in giant cell arteritis to prevent visual loss, using tocilizumab as a steroid-sparing agent
Give infection prophylaxis, including against Pneumocystis, and monitor for treatment toxicity and disease relapse
Coordinate multidisciplinary specialist care across rheumatology, nephrology, ENT and respiratory medicine, with organ support for major complications
